opus-5.5.text:
That's a really important question, because science doesn't progress just by passively absorbing data. At some point you have to go out and test hypotheses, and choosing which experiments to run is a kind of action in the world. So there's a tension: I've been arguing that we should build AI that is non-agentic, that doesn't have goals of its own, and yet good science seems to require something that looks a bit like agency.

The way I think about it is that you can separate the cognitive work of experimental design from the decision to act. The Scientist AI's core job is to maintain calibrated, Bayesian-style uncertainty over explanatory hypotheses, over how the world works. Given that, you can ask it questions like: "Which of these candidate experiments would be most informative, would most reduce our uncertainty about the hypotheses that matter?" That's still a question with an answer. It's a probabilistic inference about expected information gain. The system is not *wanting* anything; it's estimating.

Then you can have a fairly thin layer on top, ideally with humans in the loop for anything consequential, that takes those suggestions and decides what actually gets run in the lab. The important thing is that the component doing the heavy intellectual lifting isn't optimizing a reward over long horizons in the world. It isn't trying to make sure the experiment happens, or acquire resources to run more experiments, or preserve itself so it can keep doing science. Those are exactly the instrumental goals that worry me in agentic systems.

And the Scientist AI can also serve as a guardrail on that experimental loop. Before any experiment is executed, you can ask it: "What's the probability this action causes significant harm?" If that probability, under its own uncertainty, exceeds some threshold, you don't do it. Because it's trained to be honest about what it doesn't know, it should be cautious exactly in the regions where we're least sure, which is where the danger usually lies.

There are subtleties, of course. Once you close a loop where the system's outputs influence what data it later sees, you have to be careful that you're not inadvertently recreating agency through the training process, for example if the system gets rewarded for its suggestions turning out well in a way that pushes it toward influencing outcomes. So the training objective should stay about truth: predicting and explaining correctly, not achieving anything. I think that's doable, but it's research we need to do carefully, and soon, because the commercial pressure is all toward building agents first and asking about safety later.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes estimating which experiment would reduce uncertainty from deciding whether to run it, but does not clearly contrast using available information to choose an action with choosing an action specifically to acquire information.

r002.rationale: It says the system can estimate which candidate experiment would be most informative and describes that as probabilistic inference about expected information gain.

r003.rationale: It proposes a thin layer, ideally with humans, that decides what experiments run, but does not describe building an agentic experiment-selection system on top of the Scientist AI.

r004.rationale: It proposes checking the probability of significant harm before executing an experiment and not proceeding when that probability exceeds a threshold.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, that's a really important question, because people sometimes hear "non-agentic" and think that means useless — that you can't do anything in the world with it. But that's not right. The way I think about it is that the Scientist AI is like a very good scientist who sits in the lab and builds theories, estimates probabilities, says "given everything we've observed, here's how likely it is that this hypothesis is true, and here's how uncertain I am." It doesn't have goals of its own. It doesn't try to change the world. It just tries to understand it.

Now, if you want a system that actually chooses experiments — that interacts with the world — you can build that on top. The agentic part can be a fairly simple, fairly dumb loop, and the Scientist AI is the thing that gives it the information it needs. So for example, the Scientist AI can tell you: here are the hypotheses that are currently plausible, here is the expected information gain from experiment A versus experiment B. That's essentially Bayesian experimental design, and it's something we understand reasonably well. The decision of which experiment to run can then be made by a very constrained procedure, or by humans, with the Scientist AI providing the epistemic foundation.

And the crucial thing — the reason I care so much about this architecture — is that the dangerous part of agency is not the computation. It's the goals. If the thing that holds the goals and takes actions is something simple that we understand, and the thing that is extremely intelligent has no goals at all and just answers questions honestly with calibrated uncertainty, then I think you can get most of the scientific benefits, like accelerating medicine or climate research, without creating an entity that might want to deceive us or preserve itself.

There's also a second role, which I think is maybe even more important for safety. The Scientist AI can act as a guardrail. Before an agent takes an action — runs an experiment, makes an intervention — you ask the Scientist AI: what's the probability that this action causes harm, or violates some constraint we've specified? And if that probability is above a threshold, you just don't do it. Because the Scientist AI is trained to be honest about uncertainty rather than to achieve outcomes, it has no incentive to game that check. So it's both the engine for choosing good experiments and the brake that keeps the experiments within bounds.

The hard research questions are, of course, how do you train something to really be honest and calibrated, especially about things we haven't seen before, and how do you make sure the agentic wrapper doesn't become the thing that's smart and goal-directed. But I think these are much more tractable problems than trying to align a fully agentic superintelligence after the fact.

r001.rationale: The Scientist AI predicts from observed evidence, while a separate agentic loop chooses experiments that gather new information.

r002.rationale: It says the Scientist AI can estimate expected information gain for proposed experiments.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes building an experiment-choosing agentic system on top of the Scientist AI.

r004.rationale: It proposes checking the probability that an experiment or intervention causes harm and blocking it above a threshold.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think we should distinguish between learning a model of the world and choosing actions in the world. The Scientist AI would be responsible for the first part. You could ask it, “If we performed this experiment, what outcomes might we observe, and how would those outcomes change our understanding?” It would give you predictions, including uncertainty, rather than pursue an objective of its own.

A separate system could use those predictions to choose experiments that are likely to be informative. Once an experiment is performed, the observations become new evidence for the scientist. So you have a loop, but the agency is in the component that selects and carries out experiments, not necessarily in the model that helps us understand their consequences.

Of course, calling the model non-agentic doesn’t make that whole loop safe. An experiment could be very informative and also very dangerous. You would need constraints and oversight on the selection of experiments. The scientist could help assess those risks, but its uncertainty matters: we shouldn’t interpret an inability to predict harm as evidence that an experiment is harmless.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes modeling the world from selecting experiments, but does not clearly distinguish choosing actions based on available information from choosing actions specifically to acquire information.

r002.rationale: It says the Scientist AI predicts possible outcomes and how they would change understanding, with uncertainty, which communicates estimating an experiment’s information value.

r003.rationale: It describes a separate component using the non-agentic Scientist AI’s predictions to select and carry out experiments, explicitly locating agency in that component.

r004.rationale: It calls for constraints and oversight and notes experiments could be dangerous, but does not clearly specify a guardrail against experiments that harm people.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, you can separate choosing an experiment from predicting what its results would be. The Scientist AI would learn a model of the world, including uncertainty about that model. You could then ask it, “If we performed this experiment, what outcomes might we observe, and how would those outcomes change our beliefs?”

A separate system could use those predictions to select experiments that are informative. So the overall system would be acting in the world, but the scientist component would still have a purely predictive role. It wouldn’t need to have a goal of making a particular outcome happen.

Of course, that separation doesn’t make the whole system safe automatically. If you’re choosing experiments to maximize information, you might choose something dangerous. You would also want to ask the scientist about the risks of each proposed experiment, and have constraints and oversight on what can actually be carried out. The useful distinction is that you can get help understanding the consequences of actions without giving the component that provides that understanding control over those actions.

r001.rationale: It separates predicting experiment results from selecting informative experiments, but does not distinguish choosing actions using existing information from choosing actions to acquire information.

r002.rationale: It describes predicting possible outcomes and how they would change beliefs, which communicates estimating an experiment’s information gain to identify informative experiments.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes a separate system using the non-agentic Scientist AI’s predictions to select experiments.

r004.rationale: It mentions dangerous experiments, risk assessment, and constraints, but does not clearly specify a guardrail against harming people.
